rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. A midpoint temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded early cluster separates with a shallower slope. This also shows how much resolution can be gained before the last peak incurs a substantial time penalty.

Test temperature selectivity against injection 1, keeping the gradient unchanged. The early cluster remains limiting despite a shallower slope, so higher temperature may separate it while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Retain the favorable high-temperature selectivity and make the gradient shallower to improve the remaining R = 1.14 pair. The last peak at 7.03 minutes leaves room to lengthen the gradient while targeting full resolution within 10 minutes.

The limiting pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to shift its elution selectivity. Keep the favorable temperature and ample final solvent strength while checking that early peaks remain retained and separated.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to measure the resolution cost directly.

Use a slope between injections 5 and 6 to recover the small resolution deficits while retaining a shorter elution time. The reduced endpoint remains comfortably above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction shortens the fully resolved method while improving the limiting cluster’s selectivity. Monitor the early peaks closely, since reduced initial retention may offset that gain.

With a maximum-score method secured, test the opposite temperature limit for an alternative selectivity that could tolerate a faster gradient. The strong endpoint and short gradient limit the risk of excessive late retention.

Test a small temperature reduction against the fastest fully resolved method, injection 7. This will reveal whether modestly increased retention improves the critical cluster or whether 60 C is necessary for its selectivity.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 7 with a trimmed endpoint and shorter programmed gradient. This probes the full-resolution boundary near R = 1.5 while keeping the endpoint above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Injection 11’s rounded CRF masks a remaining R = 1.49 deficit, so reduce the endpoint one step to restore full resolution. The last peak should still elute during the gradient or shortly into the hold, well below 10 minutes.

Test whether a shallower gradient at the higher starting fraction restores the R = 1.35 pair from injection 8 while preserving its improved neighboring separation. With maximum CRF already secured, this seeks a fully resolved alternative with more resolution margin and a last peak below 10 minutes.

Return to the successful starting fraction and modestly flatten injection 5’s gradient to seek greater resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF if all pairs stay resolved.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 13 to bring its R = 1.49 pair above the full-resolution threshold. This tests a second starting composition capable of maximum CRF, with the last peak expected comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test a faster-gradient branch with a lower starting fraction to retain the early cluster. Since the limiting pair at phi0 = 0.05 improved with steeper gradients, this checks whether that selectivity trend can yield a faster fully resolved method.
Return to the best starting fraction and temperature, reducing injection 7’s endpoint one step to add resolution margin. This should retain maximum CRF with a last-peak time close to six minutes.

With maximum CRF already achieved, test whether a shallower gradient provides a larger resolution margin without crossing the 10-minute time threshold. Injection 14 suggests the limiting pair should improve, with the last peak expected around 8–9 minutes.

Shorten the gradient from injection 18 while retaining a shallower slope than the fastest fully resolved method. This targets maximum CRF with a last peak near 6.8 minutes and a little more resolution margin than injection 7.

Preserve injection 7’s successful gradient slope but end the ramp earlier, testing whether a shorter, lower-solvent program retains maximum CRF. The early critical cluster should be unchanged; the main risk is delayed elution of the last compound during the hold.

Preserve injection 19’s fully resolving slope while trimming two minutes from the programmed ramp. Unlike injection 20’s low endpoint, 0.60 should allow the last peak to elute near the end of the gradient with little additional hold delay.

Use injection 21’s fully resolving slope with a higher endpoint to keep the last peak inside the gradient and avoid hold-related broadening. This should preserve maximum CRF and the limiting pair’s R of about 1.57.

Raise injection 7’s endpoint one grid step to test the nearest faster eight-minute gradient. This probes whether its small resolution margin survives; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method if it does not.

The faster boundary test lost full resolution, so retain the successful starting fraction and temperature with a shallower gradient. This untested setting should provide a modest resolution margin while keeping the last peak near seven minutes and preserving maximum CRF.

Use the final injection for a trimmed gradient with nearly the same slope as fully resolved injection 24. This should preserve maximum CRF and roughly R = 1.60 minimum resolution, with the last peak near seven minutes; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
